claims.text: HEA-alloyed Q235 steel forms an oxide layer enriched in HEA elements.
The HEA-enriched oxide layer is stable across room- and high-temperature regimes.
The HEA-enriched oxide layer adheres to Q235 steel.
Formation of the stable, adherent, HEA-enriched oxide layer governs corrosion protection in Q235 steel.
Alloying Q235 steel with HEA elements alters the composition of its oxide layer.
Alloying Q235 steel with HEA elements alters the microstructure of its oxide layer.
The HEA-induced changes in oxide composition and microstructure enhance the oxide layer's protective properties.
The HEA-induced changes in oxide composition and microstructure enhance the oxide layer's thermal stability.
HEA-alloyed Q235 steel will have greater corrosion resistance than unalloyed Q235 steel during aggressive-salt exposure at 700–900 °C.
HEA-alloyed Q235 steel will exhibit less mass change than unalloyed Q235 steel during aggressive-salt exposure at 700–900 °C.
HEA-alloyed Q235 steel will retain more hardness than unalloyed Q235 steel after aggressive-salt exposure at 700–900 °C.
Annealed HEA-alloyed Q235 samples will perform better than corresponding non-annealed samples.
Annealing at 1000 °C for 2 hours promotes the proposed protective behavior of HEA-alloyed Q235 steel.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis claims protection across room- and high-temperature regimes, but the stated exposure conditions and falsification experiment assess only aggressive-salt exposure at 700–900 °C and include no room-temperature corrosion test.
